plan.topic_summary: Mixture of Experts (MoE) is a sparse model architecture that routes inputs to subsets of specialized sub-networks, enabling large parameter counts at reduced per-token compute. For a 1–5 year view, the key question is whether MoE becomes the default scaling paradigm for frontier models or remains a niche trade-off, and how its cost, stability, and deployment characteristics evolve relative to dense alternatives.
key_questions: What is the current state of MoE adoption in production LLMs, and what are the primary barriers (memory, tooling, serving infrastructure) to broader deployment in the next 12 months?
How is the inference cost of MoE models trending relative to dense models of comparable quality, and at what parameter scale does MoE become the cost-optimal choice over the next 1–3 years?
What progress is being made on training stability (load balancing, expert collapse) and does it constrain the maximum practical model size or the rate of scaling?
Are there architectural or hardware-level alternatives (e.g., new sparsity paradigms, native sparse accelerators) that could displace or subsume MoE as the dominant scaling approach over 3–5 years?
How does MoE interact with emerging deployment constraints such as edge inference, multi-modal workloads, and agentic tool-calling loops, and does it remain suitable for those use cases?

gaps: Theoretical grounding is thin: only one paper (S6, low confidence) addresses convergence/identifiability, leaving the fundamental mathematical properties of MoE underexplored.
Soft MoE as an architectural alternative rests on a single paper (S4); no comparative evidence against sparse MoE at scale is present.
Most risk findings (R3, R8) note that proposed fixes are validated only at small or narrow scale; production-scale evidence for MoE reliability remains limited.
Market evidence (M1–M5) confirms commercial adoption but provides no detail on realized production performance, cost savings, or failure rates at scale.

sources.title: A Survey on Mixture of Experts in Large Language Models
sources.venue: IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering
sources.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have garnered unprecedented advancements across diverse fields, ranging from natural language processing to computer vision and beyond. The prowess of LLMs is underpinned by their substantial model size, extensive and diverse datasets, and the vast computational power harnessed during training, all of which contribute to the emergent abilities of LLMs (e.g., in-context learning) that are not present in small models. Within this context, the mixture of experts (MoE) has emerged as an effective method for substantially scaling up model capacity with minimal computation overhead, gaining significant attention from academia and industry. Despite its growing prevalence, there lacks a systematic and comprehensive review of the literature on MoE. This survey seeks to bridge that gap, serving as an essential resource for researchers delving into the intricacies of MoE. We first briefly introduce the structure of the MoE layer, followed by proposing a new taxonomy of MoE. Next, we overview the core designs for various MoE models including both algorithmic and systemic aspects, alongside collections of available open-source implementations, hyperparameter configurations and empirical evaluations. Furthermore, we delineate the multifaceted applications of MoE in practice, and outline some potential directions for future research.

sources.title: Not All Experts are Equal: Efficient Expert Pruning and Skipping for Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models
sources.abstract: A pivotal advancement in the progress of large language models (LLMs) is the emergence of the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs. Compared to traditional LLMs, MoE LLMs can achieve higher performance with fewer parameters, but it is still hard to deploy them due to their immense parameter sizes. Different from previous weight pruning methods that rely on specifically designed hardware, this paper mainly aims to enhance the deployment efficiency of MoE LLMs by introducing plug-and-play expert-level sparsification techniques. Specifically, we propose, for the first time to our best knowledge, post-training approaches for task-agnostic and task-specific expert pruning and skipping of MoE LLMs, tailored to improve deployment efficiency while maintaining model performance across a wide range of tasks. Extensive experiments show that our proposed methods can simultaneously reduce model sizes and increase the inference speed, while maintaining satisfactory performance. Data and code will be available at https://github.com/Lucky-Lance/Expert_Sparsity.

sources.title: OLMoE: Open Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
sources.abstract: We introduce OLMoE, a fully open, state-of-the-art language model leveraging sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE). OLMoE-1B-7B has 7 billion (B) parameters but uses only 1B per input token. We pretrain it on 5 trillion tokens and further adapt it to create OLMoE-1B-7B-Instruct. Our models outperform all available models with similar active parameters, even surpassing larger ones like Llama2-13B-Chat and DeepSeekMoE-16B. We present various experiments on MoE training, analyze routing in our model showing high specialization, and open-source all aspects of our work: model weights, training data, code, and logs.

sources.title: ExpertFlow: Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Inference via Predictive Expert Caching and Token Scheduling
sources.abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models can outperform dense large language models at similar computation by activating only a small set of experts per token. However, stacking many expert modules introduces substantial parameter memory, which makes MoE models difficult to deploy in memory-constrained environments such as single-GPU devices. Offloading alleviates this issue by storing inactive experts in CPU memory and loading them on demand, but existing methods remain limited: static caches disregard input-dependent routing, and methods that train separate models to predict expert usage ahead of time are often inaccurate or require significant training cost. We propose ExpertFlow, a lightweight MoE inference system that addresses this routing dependency through three coordinated components: 1) a transformer-based routing path predictor that estimates expert usage across all MoE layers in a single forward pass, 2) a token scheduler that groups tokens with similar predicted routes to improve expert utilization, and 3) a predictive expert cache that loads only the required experts while correcting mispredictions at runtime. Together, these components enable efficient expert loading and execution, reducing GPU memory usage by up to 93.72% and improving inference throughput by up to 10x over strong offloading baselines on a single GPU.

sources.title: DeepSeekMoE: Towards Ultimate Expert Specialization in Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
sources.venue: Proceedings of the conference - Association for Computational Linguistics. Meeting
sources.abstract: In the era of large language models, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a promising architecture for managing computational costs when scaling up model parameters. However, conventional MoE architectures like GShard, which activate the top- K out of N experts, face challenges in ensuring expert specialization, i.e. each expert acquires non-overlapping and focused knowledge. In response, we propose the DeepSeekMoE architecture towards ultimate expert specialization. It involves two principal strategies: (1) finely segmenting the experts into mN ones and activating mK from them, allowing for a more flexible combination of activated experts; (2) isolating K s experts as shared ones, aiming at capturing common knowledge and mitigating redundancy in routed experts. Starting from a modest scale with 2B parameters, we demonstrate that DeepSeekMoE 2B achieves comparable performance with GShard 2.9B, which has 1.5 × expert parameters and computation. In addition, DeepSeekMoE 2B nearly approaches the performance of its dense counterpart with the same number of total parameters, which sets the upper bound of MoE models. Subsequently, we scale up DeepSeekMoE to 16B parameters and show that it achieves comparable performance with DeepSeek 7B and LLaMA2 7B, with only about 40% of computations.

sources.title: Convergence Rates for Softmax Gating Mixture of Experts
sources.abstract: Mixture of experts (MoE) has recently emerged as an effective framework to advance the efficiency and scalability of machine learning models by softly dividing complex tasks among multiple specialized sub-models termed experts. Central to the success of MoE is an adaptive softmax gating mechanism which takes responsibility for determining the relevance of each expert to a given input and then dynamically assigning experts their respective weights. Despite its widespread use in practice, a comprehensive study on the effects of the softmax gating on the MoE has been lacking in the literature. To bridge this gap in this paper, we perform a convergence analysis of parameter estimation and expert estimation under the MoE equipped with the standard softmax gating or its variants, including a dense-to-sparse gating and a hierarchical softmax gating, respectively. Furthermore, our theories also provide useful insights into the design of sample-efficient expert structures. In particular, we demonstrate that it requires polynomially many data points to estimate experts satisfying our proposed \emph{strong identifiability} condition, namely a commonly used two-layer feed-forward network. In stark contrast, estimating linear experts, which violate the strong identifiability condition, necessitates exponentially many data points as a result of intrinsic parameter interactions expressed in the language of partial differential equations. All the theoretical results are substantiated with a rigorous guarantee.

sources.title: Scaling Laws for Fine-Grained Mixture of Experts
sources.abstract: Mixture of Experts (MoE) models have emerged as a primary solution for reducing the computational cost of Large Language Models. In this work, we analyze their scaling properties, incorporating an expanded range of variables. Specifically, we introduce a new hyperparameter, granularity, whose adjustment enables precise control over the size of the experts. Building on this, we establish scaling laws for fine-grained MoE, taking into account the number of training tokens, model size, and granularity. Leveraging these laws, we derive the optimal training configuration for a given computational budget. Our findings not only show that MoE models consistently outperform dense Transformers but also highlight that the efficiency gap between dense and MoE models widens as we scale up the model size and training budget. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the common practice of setting the size of experts in MoE to mirror the feed-forward layer is not optimal at almost any computational budget.

sources.title: Mixture-of-Experts Models in Vision: Routing, Optimization, and Generalization
sources.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable conditional computation by routing inputs to multiple expert subnetworks and are often motivated as a mechanism for scaling large language models. In this project, we instead study MoE behavior in an image classification setting, focusing on predictive performance, expert utilization, and generalization. We compare dense, SoftMoE, and SparseMoE classifier heads on the CIFAR10 dataset under comparable model capacity. Both MoE variants achieve slightly higher validation accuracy than the dense baseline while maintaining balanced expert utilization through regularization, avoiding expert collapse. To analyze generalization, we compute Hessian-based sharpness metrics at convergence, including the largest eigenvalue and trace of the loss Hessian, evaluated on both training and test data. We find that SoftMoE exhibits higher sharpness by these metrics, while Dense and SparseMoE lie in a similar curvature regime, despite all models achieving comparable generalization performance. Complementary loss surface perturbation analyses reveal qualitative differences in non-local behavior under finite parameter perturbations between dense and MoE models, which help contextualize curvature-based measurements without directly explaining validation accuracy. We further evaluate empirical inference efficiency and show that naively implemented conditional routing does not yield inference speedups on modern hardware at this scale, highlighting the gap between theoretical and realized efficiency in sparse MoE models.

sources.title: From Sparse to Soft Mixtures of Experts
sources.abstract: Sparse mixture of expert architectures (MoEs) scale model capacity without significant increases in training or inference costs. Despite their success, MoEs suffer from a number of issues: training instability, token dropping, inability to scale the number of experts, or ineffective finetuning. In this work, we propose Soft MoE, a fully-differentiable sparse Transformer that addresses these challenges, while maintaining the benefits of MoEs. Soft MoE performs an implicit soft assignment by passing different weighted combinations of all input tokens to each expert. As in other MoEs, experts in Soft MoE only process a subset of the (combined) tokens, enabling larger model capacity (and performance) at lower inference cost. In the context of visual recognition, Soft MoE greatly outperforms dense Transformers (ViTs) and popular MoEs (Tokens Choice and Experts Choice). Furthermore, Soft MoE scales well: Soft MoE Huge/14 with 128 experts in 16 MoE layers has over 40x more parameters than ViT Huge/14, with only 2% increased inference time, and substantially better quality.

sources.title: Task-Conditioned Routing Signatures in Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Transformers
sources.abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable efficient scaling of large language models through conditional computation, yet the routing mechanisms responsible for expert selection remain poorly understood. In this work, we introduce routing signatures, a vector representation summarizing expert activation patterns across layers for a given prompt, and use them to study whether MoE routing exhibits task-conditioned structure. Using OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-Instruct as an empirical testbed, we show that prompts from the same task category induce highly similar routing signatures, while prompts from different categories exhibit substantially lower similarity. Within-category routing similarity (0.8435 +/- 0.0879) significantly exceeds across-category similarity (0.6225 +/- 0.1687), corresponding to Cohen's d = 1.44. A logistic regression classifier trained solely on routing signatures achieves 92.5% +/- 6.1% cross-validated accuracy on four-way task classification. To ensure statistical validity, we introduce permutation and load-balancing baselines and show that the observed separation is not explained by sparsity or balancing constraints alone. We further analyze layer-wise signal strength and low-dimensional projections of routing signatures, finding that task structure becomes increasingly apparent in deeper layers. These results suggest that routing in sparse transformers is not merely a balancing mechanism, but a measurable task-sensitive component of conditional computation. We release MOE-XRAY, a lightweight toolkit for routing telemetry and analysis.

sources.title: Interpretable Mixture of Experts
sources.abstract: The need for reliable model explanations is prominent for many machine learning applications, particularly for tabular and time-series data as their use cases often involve high-stakes decision making. Towards this goal, we introduce a novel interpretable modeling framework, Interpretable Mixture of Experts (IME), that yields high accuracy, comparable to `black-box' Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) in many cases, along with useful interpretability capabilities. IME consists of an assignment module and a mixture of experts, with each sample being assigned to a single expert for prediction. We introduce multiple options for IME based on the assignment and experts being interpretable. When the experts are chosen to be interpretable such as linear models, IME yields an inherently-interpretable architecture where the explanations produced by IME are the exact descriptions of how the prediction is computed. In addition to constituting a standalone inherently-interpretable architecture, IME has the premise of being integrated with existing DNNs to offer interpretability to a subset of samples while maintaining the accuracy of the DNNs. Through extensive experiments on 15 tabular and time-series datasets, IME is demonstrated to be more accurate than single interpretable models and perform comparably with existing state-of-the-art DNNs in accuracy. On most datasets, IME even outperforms DNNs, while providing faithful explanations. Lastly, IME's explanations are compared to commonly-used post-hoc explanations methods through a user study -- participants are able to better predict the model behavior when given IME explanations, while finding IME's explanations more faithful and trustworthy.

sources.title: GEM: Graph-Enhanced Mixture-of-Experts with ReAct Agents for Dialogue State Tracking
sources.abstract: Dialogue State Tracking (DST) requires precise extraction of structured information from multi-domain conversations, a task where Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle despite their impressive general capabilities. We present GEM (Graph-Enhanced Mixture-of-Experts), a novel framework that combines language models and graph-structured dialogue understanding with ReAct agent-based reasoning for superior DST performance. Our approach dynamically routes between specialized experts: a Graph Neural Network that captures dialogue structure and turn-level dependencies, and a finetuned T5-Small encoder-decoder for sequence modeling, coordinated by an intelligent router. For complex value generation tasks, we integrate ReAct agents that perform structured reasoning over dialogue context. On MultiWOZ 2.2, GEM achieves 65.19% Joint Goal Accuracy, substantially outperforming end-to-end LLM approaches (best: 38.43%) and surpassing state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods including TOATOD (63.79%), D3ST (58.70%), and Diable (56.48%). Our graph-enhanced mixture-of-experts architecture with ReAct integration demonstrates that combining structured dialogue representation with dynamic expert routing and agent-based reasoning provides a powerful paradigm for dialogue state tracking, achieving superior accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency through selective expert activation.

sources.title: LLaMA-MoE: Building Mixture-of-Experts from LLaMA with Continual Pre-Training
sources.venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
sources.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has gained increasing popularity as a promising framework for scaling up large language models (LLMs). However, training MoE from scratch in a large-scale setting still suffers from data-hungry and instability problems. Motivated by this limit, we investigate building MoE models from existing dense large language models. Specifically, based on the well-known LLaMA-2 7B model, we obtain an MoE model by: (1) Expert Construction, which partitions the parameters of original Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) into multiple experts; (2) Continual pre-training, which further trains the transformed MoE model and additional gate networks. In this paper, we comprehensively explore different methods for expert construction and various data sampling strategies for continual pre-training. After these stages, our LLaMA-MoE models could maintain language abilities and route the input tokens to specific experts with part of the parameters activated. Empirically, by training 200B tokens, LLaMA-MoE-3.5B models significantly outperform dense models that contain similar activation parameters.

sources.title: Mixture of Experts with Soft Nearest Neighbor Loss: Resolving Expert Collapse via Representation Disentanglement
sources.abstract: The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model uses a set of expert networks that specialize on subsets of a dataset under the supervision of a gating network. A common issue in MoE architectures is ``expert collapse'' where overlapping class boundaries in the raw input feature space cause multiple experts to learn redundant representations, thus forcing the gating network into rigid routing to compensate. We propose an enhanced MoE architecture that utilizes a feature extractor network optimized using Soft Nearest Neighbor Loss (SNNL) prior to feeding input features to the gating and expert networks. By pre-conditioning the latent space to minimize distances among class-similar data points, we resolve structural expert collapse which results to experts learning highly orthogonal weights. We employ Expert Specialization Entropy and Pairwise Embedding Similarity to quantify this dynamic. We evaluate our experimental approach across four benchmark image classification datasets (MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100), and we show our SNNL-augmented MoE models demonstrate structurally diverse experts which allow the gating network to adopt a more flexible routing strategy. This paradigm significantly improves classification accuracy on the FashionMNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 datasets.

sources.title: Stabilizing MoE Reinforcement Learning by Aligning Training and Inference Routers
sources.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a crucial approach for enhancing the capabilities of large language models. However, in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, the routing mechanism often introduces instability, even leading to catastrophic RL training collapse. We analyze the training-inference consistency of MoE models and identify a notable discrepancy in routing behaviors between the two phases. Moreover, even under identical conditions, the routing framework can yield divergent expert selections across repeated forward passes. To address this foundational inconsistency, we propose Rollout Routing Replay (R3), a method that records routing distributions from the inference engine and replays them during training. R3 significantly reduces training-inference policy KL divergence and mitigates extreme discrepancies without compromising training speed. Extensive experiments on various settings confirm that R3 succeeds in stabilizing RL training, preventing collapse and outperforming methods such as GSPO and TIS. We believe this work can offer a new solution for stabilizing RL in MoE models.

sources.title: Rethinking Gating Mechanism in Sparse MoE: Handling Arbitrary Modality Inputs with Confidence-Guided Gate
sources.abstract: Effectively managing missing modalities is a fundamental challenge in real-world multimodal learning scenarios, where data incompleteness often results from systematic collection errors or sensor failures. Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) architectures have the potential to naturally handle multimodal data, with individual experts specializing in different modalities. However, existing SMoE approach often lacks proper ability to handle missing modality, leading to performance degradation and poor generalization in real-world applications. We propose ConfSMoE to introduce a two-stage imputation module to handle the missing modality problem for the SMoE architecture by taking the opinion of experts and reveal the insight of expert collapse from theoretical analysis with strong empirical evidence. Inspired by our theoretical analysis, ConfSMoE propose a novel expert gating mechanism by detaching the softmax routing score to task confidence score w.r.t ground truth signal. This naturally relieves expert collapse without introducing additional load balance loss function. We show that the insights of expert collapse aligns with other gating mechanism such as Gaussian and Laplacian gate. The proposed method is evaluated on four different real world dataset with three distinct experiment settings to conduct comprehensive analysis of ConfSMoE on resistance to missing modality and the impacts of proposed gating mechanism.

sources.title: Probing RLVR training instability through the lens of objective-level hacking
sources.abstract: Prolonged reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has been shown to drive continuous improvements in the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but the training is often prone to instabilities, especially in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures. Training instability severely undermines model capability improvement, yet its underlying causes and mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we introduce a principled framework for understanding RLVR instability through the lens of objective-level hacking. Unlike reward hacking, which arises from exploitable verifiers, objective-level hacking emerges from token-level credit misalignment and is manifested as system-level spurious signals in the optimization objective. Grounded in our framework, together with extensive experiments on a 30B MoE model, we trace the origin and formalize the mechanism behind a key pathological training dynamic in MoE models: the abnormal growth of the training-inference discrepancy, a phenomenon widely associated with instability but previously lacking a mechanistic explanation. These findings provide a concrete and causal account of the training dynamics underlying instabilities in MoE models, offering guidance for the design of stable RLVR algorithms.

sources.title: Function Over Form: Distributional Orthogonalization in Mixture-of-Experts with Replica Expert Mechanism
sources.abstract: The scaling of LLMs increasingly relies on MoE architectures to decouple active computation from total parameter count. However, the efficacy of MoE is often constrained by expert collapse and representation redundancy, both leading to underutilization of model capacity. To address these challenges, this paper proposes Distributional Orthogonalization Loss (DO-loss), an auxiliary regularization that shifts the focus from static weight diversity to dynamic routing behavior. By representing each expert's token assignment history as a high-dimensional binary load signature, DO-loss penalizes signature overlap to prevent expert collapse while encouraging functional specialization. To align this algorithmic design with system efficiency, we further introduce the Replica Expert Mechanism (REM), which improves load balancing through a two-tiered strategy: adjusting replica expert placement at the global-batch level and performing real-time token dispatching at the micro-batch level. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our method outperforms the evaluated routing algorithms on downstream tasks for both 4.8BA0.5B and 30BA3B MoE models, while maintaining comparable training efficiency.

sources.title: Sparse Backpropagation for MoE Training
sources.abstract: One defining characteristic of Mixture-of-Expert (MoE) models is their capacity for conducting sparse computation via expert routing, leading to remarkable scalability. However, backpropagation, the cornerstone of deep learning, requires dense computation, thereby posting challenges in MoE gradient computations. Here, we introduce SparseMixer, a scalable gradient estimator that bridges the gap between backpropagation and sparse expert routing. Unlike typical MoE training which strategically neglects certain gradient terms for the sake of sparse computation and scalability, SparseMixer provides scalable gradient approximations for these terms, enabling reliable gradient estimation in MoE training. Grounded in a numerical ODE framework, SparseMixer harnesses the mid-point method, a second-order ODE solver, to deliver precise gradient approximations with negligible computational overhead. Applying SparseMixer to Switch Transformer on both pre-training and machine translation tasks, SparseMixer showcases considerable performance gain, accelerating training convergence up to 2 times.

sources.title: Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts: Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds
sources.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts models rely on learned routers to assign tokens to experts, yet standard softmax gating provides no principled mechanism to control the tradeoff between sparsity and utilization. We propose Grassmannian MoE (GrMoE), a routing framework that operates on the Grassmannian manifold of subspaces, where gating weights arise from the concentration parameters of Matrix Bingham distributions. This construction yields a single, interpretable knob -- the concentration matrix $Λ$ -- that continuously controls routing entropy, replacing discrete top-$k$ selection with a smooth, geometrically principled sparsity mechanism. We further develop an amortized variational inference procedure for posterior routing distributions, enabling uncertainty-aware expert assignment that naturally resists expert collapse. We formally prove tight bounds relating the Bingham concentration spectrum to routing entropy, expected top-$k$ mass, and an exponential bound on expert collapse, establishing the first formal theory of concentration-controlled sparsity. On synthetic routing tasks, a 350M-parameter MoE language model with 8 experts, a 1.3B-parameter model with 16 experts, and a 2.7B-parameter model with 32 experts, GrMoE achieves 0\% routing collapse across all seeds, comparable or better perplexity with 15--30\% improved load balance, and a smooth monotonic relationship between concentration and effective sparsity that enables post-hoc sparsity tuning without retraining. Token-level analysis reveals that experts learn heterogeneous concentration values that correlate with linguistic specialization, providing interpretable routing behavior.

sources.title: Grouter: Decoupling Routing from Representation for Accelerated MoE Training
sources.abstract: Traditional Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) training typically proceeds without any structural priors, effectively requiring the model to simultaneously train expert weights while searching for an optimal routing policy within a vast combinatorial space. This entanglement often leads to sluggish convergence and training instabilities. This paper introduces Grouter, a preemptive routing method that by distilling high-quality structures from fully-trained MoE models and serving as a fixed router for target models. By decoupling structural optimization from weight updates, Grouter significantly accelerates both the speed and quality of model convergence. To ensure the framework's versatility, we also introduce expert folding to adapt Grouter across varying model configurations and expert tuning to rebalance workloads across different data distributions. Furthermore, by leveraging the structural priors provided by preemptive routing, we can implement targeted optimizations to further enhance training throughput. Experiments demonstrate that Grouter achieves superior performance and efficiency which boosts pre-training data utilization by 4.28x and achieves up to 33.5% throughput acceleration, establishing preemptive routing as a fundamental paradigm for scalable MoE training. We publicly release our code and pretrained Grouter checkpoints at https://github.com/JimmyAwoe/Grouter.

sources.title: AdapterMoE: A Two-Stage Hard-Routing Mixture-of-Experts Architecture for Multi-Crop Disease Recognition with Calibrated Rejection and Incremental Learning
sources.abstract: Timely crop-disease identification is critical to food security. Multi-crop recognition suits Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), but conventional soft-routing MoE learns crop assignment freely end-to-end, letting a few experts dominate (expert collapse) with no semantic correspondence to crops, and facing high retraining costs, unstable rejection of non-target inputs, and a saturated accuracy ceiling. We shift the objective from accuracy toward a trade-off among deployment cost, scaling flexibility, and rejection stability, using deterministic hard routing. We propose AdapterMoE: a RouterHead classifies the crop and rejects non-target crops via a Maximum Softmax Probability threshold, with a dual-gate Energy+KNN out-of-distribution module catching distribution-shifted inputs; five per-crop Adapters atop a frozen EfficientNet-B0 backbone discriminate diseases, each calibrated via Temperature Scaling. Because experts are hard-isolated at the data level, the design avoids expert collapse and exposes an add_crop interface for local, per-crop updates instead of full retraining. On PlantVillage (5 crops, 26 classes), across a fair five-system comparison, AdapterMoE attains accuracy statistically indistinguishable from the best baselines (Macro-F1 within a 0.24-point band) while cutting training cost to about 9% of full-network baselines, expanding to a new crop in

sources.title: EAQuant: Enhancing Post-Training Quantization for MoE Models via Expert-Aware Optimization
sources.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models enable scalable computation and performance in large-scale deep learning but face quantization challenges due to sparse expert activation and dynamic routing. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods fail to address activation outliers, routing instability, and sparse expert calibration, leading to significant performance degradation. To address this, we propose EAQuant, a PTQ framework tailored for MoE architectures. Our method introduces three expert-aware innovations: (1) smoothing aggregation to suppress activation outliers, (2) routing consistency alignment to preserve expert selection post-quantization, and (3) calibration data balance to optimize sparsely activated experts. These strategies collectively enable robust, high-precision quantization of MoE models under ultra-low-bit constraints.Extensive experiments across several extreme quantization settings (e.g., W4A4/W3A4/W3A3/W2A4) demonstrate that EAQuant significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving average accuracy improvements of 1.15 - 13.81% across three diverse MoE architectures, with particularly pronounced gains in reasoning tasks and robust performance retention under aggressive quantization. By integrating these innovations, EAQuant establishes a new state-of-the-art for high-precision, efficient MoE model compression.Our code is available at https://github.com/darren-fzq1/EAQuant.

sources.title: Distillation-based Scenario-Adaptive Mixture-of-Experts for the Matching Stage of Multi-scenario Recommendation
sources.abstract: Multi-scenario recommendation is pivotal for optimizing user experience across diverse contexts. While Multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts (MMOE) thrives in ranking, its transfer to the matching stage is hindered by the blind optimization inherent to independent two-tower architectures and the parameter dominance of head scenarios. To address these structural and distributional bottlenecks, we propose Distillation-based Scenario-Adaptive Mixture-of-Experts (DSMOE). Specially, we devise a Scenario-Adaptive Projection (SAP) module to generate lightweight, context-specific parameters, effectively preventing expert collapse in long-tail scenarios. Concurrently, we introduce a cross-architecture knowledge distillation framework, where an interaction-aware teacher guides the two-tower student to capture complex matching patterns. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate DSMOE's superiority, particularly in significantly improving retrieval quality for under-represented, data-sparse scenarios.

findings.claim: MoE reinforcement learning (RL) training is prone to instability and even collapse. One paper reports that routing differs between inference and training, and that repeated forward passes can select different experts under identical conditions.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: Two ICML-listed abstracts point the same way: one identifies the training-inference routing mismatch, the other traces the growing training-inference discrepancy in a 30B MoE. The R3 fix is a patch that needs inference-engine routing to be recorded and replayed. Whether this generalizes beyond the tested settings is not shown in the abstracts.
findings.supporting_excerpt: in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, the routing mechanism often introduces instability, even leading to catastrophic RL training collapse.

findings.claim: The mechanism behind MoE RL instability was described as poorly understood until recently. A 'mechanistic explanation' was reported as previously lacking, so current stabilization methods may be partial or empirical workarounds.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The abstract of src_43b4fe1915 says the abnormal growth of the training-inference discrepancy was 'previously lacking a mechanistic explanation'. src_5d11bc2465 proposes a different fix (route replay), and the two papers frame the root cause differently (routing inconsistency vs. token-level credit misalignment). The fact that causal accounts differ suggests the field has not settled on one. Abstract-only evidence; the papers' claims are not compared here in detail.

findings.claim: Expert collapse (redundant or underused experts and rigid routing) is a recurring, unresolved failure mode in MoE. Many different papers propose different remedies, and none is shown here to be established as standard.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Six papers, mostly arXiv preprints (not peer reviewed), each name expert collapse as a problem and each propose a different fix (SNNL pre-conditioning, confidence gating, DO-loss, Grassmannian routing, hard routing, scenario-adaptive projection). The variety suggests no consensus fix. Several are evaluated on small tasks (MNIST/CIFAR, PlantVillage), which limits relevance to frontier LLMs.

findings.claim: Training MoE from scratch at large scale is described as data-hungry and unstable, and the conversion of dense models into MoE is proposed as a way around it. Conversion results come from a single 7B base model and 200B training tokens.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The LLaMA-MoE abstract states the from-scratch limitation. Grouter also says unstructured joint learning of routing and weights 'often leads to sluggish convergence and training instabilities'. The LLaMA-MoE comparison is only against dense models of similar active parameters, at a single small scale; it does not show parity with larger models.
findings.supporting_excerpt: training MoE from scratch in a large-scale setting still suffers from data-hungry and instability problems.

findings.claim: Standard MoE training uses approximations that the abstracts say are imperfect. Sparse expert routing conflicts with dense backpropagation, so some gradient terms are neglected, which may limit training quality or speed.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: Single 2023 arXiv-hosted abstract; the claim concerns the typical practice at that time and may have been superseded. The reported improvement (up to 2x convergence) is on Switch Transformer only.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Unlike typical MoE training which strategically neglects certain gradient terms for the sake of sparse computation and scalability

findings.claim: MoE models are harder to compress by post-training quantization: sparse expert activation, activation outliers, and routing instability cause significant degradation under existing PTQ methods, which creates a deployment-cost risk for the 'cheap active compute' value claim.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: Based on a single preprint abstract (not peer reviewed); the authors' own method is claimed to fix this, so the problem's residual severity is unclear. Gains of 1.15-13.81% accuracy over baselines imply baselines lost substantial accuracy in extreme-bit settings (W4A4 and below), which are aggressive.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods fail to address activation outliers, routing instability, and sparse expert calibration, leading to significant performance degradation.

findings.claim: MoE load balancing and system efficiency remain a coupled algorithm/systems problem. Routing fixes often need extra mechanisms (replica experts, fixed pre-trained routers, auxiliary losses) that add complexity and dependence on a pre-trained teacher MoE.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Grouter distills routing from a fully trained MoE, so it needs one to exist first; the DO-loss/REM paper adds placement and dispatch machinery. Results are for 4.8BA0.5B and 30BA3B models, with gains described relative to 'evaluated routing algorithms' only. No evidence on frontier-scale clusters is given in these abstracts.

findings.claim: Several MoE improvements are validated only at small or narrow scale, such as image classification on MNIST/CIFAR, a five-crop plant dataset, or models up to 2.7B parameters. Their relevance to production-scale LLM MoE is unproven.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: These are arXiv preprints, not peer reviewed. GrMoE reports tests on synthetic tasks and 350M-2.7B models; the SNNL paper uses four small image datasets; AdapterMoE uses PlantVillage and explicitly accepts a 'saturated accuracy ceiling'. This is a gap in evidence for scale, not proof of failure.

hype_flags: 'Establishes a new state-of-the-art' (EAQuant): based on the authors' own benchmarks in a preprint, with accuracy gains reported as an average range
'First formal theory of concentration-controlled sparsity' and '0% routing collapse' (GrMoE): preprint with small models (up to 2.7B) and some synthetic tasks
'Fundamental paradigm for scalable MoE training' (Grouter): strong framing for a method that depends on a pre-trained MoE and is shown in limited settings
'Remarkable scalability' of sparse computation: abstracts also describe unresolved training instability, routing and quantization problems
'Resolve expert collapse' claims on MNIST/CIFAR-scale image classification, which may not carry over to LLM-scale MoE

finding.claim: S1 states that MoE gives capacity with "proportionally lower computation" and that the advantage keeps widening. The cited evidence is narrower. The widening gap comes from fitted scaling laws in a single preprint and is stated in training compute terms. The DeepSeekMoE abstract frames the dense model with the same total parameters as the upper bound for MoE. S1 also leaves out the memory, communication and deployment costs that S3, S10 and R6 show are real.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstracts support an efficiency advantage per unit of training compute within the fitted range. They do not support 'proportionally lower computation' as a general claim, and they say nothing about extrapolation beyond the fitted range or about wall-clock cost. Rated high-confidence 'verified_fact' in S1, this is overstated.
finding.supporting_excerpt: DeepSeekMoE 2B nearly approaches the performance of its dense counterpart with the same number of total parameters, which sets the upper bound of MoE models.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S10 generalises a gap between theoretical and realised speedup from a small CIFAR10 image-classification project. That project uses MoE classifier heads and a naive routing implementation. It is a single 2026 preprint. It is weak evidence about LLM-scale MoE inference. Soft MoE's abstract reports only 2% added inference time at a huge scale, which points the other way.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: S10 hedges with 'at small model scales', but the 'modern hardware' framing implies broader relevance. The result concerns naive implementations on a toy task, not optimised MoE serving systems.
finding.supporting_excerpt: We compare dense, SoftMoE, and SparseMoE classifier heads on the CIFAR10 dataset under comparable model capacity.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S11 says OLMoE-1B-7B outperforms larger dense models such as Llama2-13B-Chat. The abstract gives OLMoE's 5T-token pretraining budget but no matched training budget or compute for the comparison models. The result is self-reported by the model's authors. 'Only 1B active parameters' leaves out that all 7B parameters must be held in memory. The comparison may therefore reflect training data volume as much as architecture.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract does not control for training tokens or compute across baselines, and it does not say which benchmarks were used. 'Outperform' is therefore not shown to be an architectural advantage.
finding.supporting_excerpt: We pretrain it on 5 trillion tokens and further adapt it to create OLMoE-1B-7B-Instruct.

finding.claim: S4 says Soft MoE solves training instability, token dropping and expert scaling. The only supporting evidence is the authors' own abstract, which reports results in visual recognition. It gives no isolated evidence for each claimed fix. The finding also does not mention that these claims are not shown for language modelling, where most MoE deployment interest lies (S1, S11).
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract lists the problems and asserts the method 'addresses these challenges'. It gives no quantified evidence on stability or token dropping. The scope is vision only.
finding.supporting_excerpt: In the context of visual recognition, Soft MoE greatly outperforms dense Transformers (ViTs) and popular MoEs (Tokens Choice and Experts Choice).
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S5 draws a general conclusion about routing in sparse transformers from one small model, OLMoE-1B-7B-Instruct, one preprint and a four-way task classification. The similarity could reflect input distribution or lexical similarity within a task category, not a task-sensitive routing mechanism. The abstract's baselines only rule out sparsity and load balancing.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The generalisation 'MoE routing in sparse transformers' goes beyond a single-model study. The causal reading ('task-sensitive component') is an interpretation, yet S5 is labelled verified_fact.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Using OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-Instruct as an empirical testbed, we show that prompts from the same task category induce highly similar routing signatures
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S7 treats the use of MoE in vision, tabular data and dialogue as one trend. The cited works use different meanings of 'MoE'. GEM routes between a GNN and a T5-Small model, a heterogeneous model ensemble. IME assigns each sample to a single interpretable expert. Neither is a sparse-FFN transformer MoE as in S1/S2/S11. The evidence for broad applicability of the LLM-style architecture is therefore weaker than S7 suggests.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Heterogeneous expert ensembles and CIFAR10 heads are different from large sparse MoE layers. Calling this 'MoE applied beyond NLP' conflates the architectures. GEM and the vision study are also single preprints.
finding.supporting_excerpt: a Graph Neural Network that captures dialogue structure and turn-level dependencies, and a finetuned T5-Small encoder-decoder for sequence modeling, coordinated by an intelligent router

finding.claim: S12 and S3 present ExpertFlow's best-case numbers as evidence that consumer-hardware MoE deployment is becoming feasible. The abstract's figures are 'up to' values against the authors' chosen offloading baselines, from a single preprint. 'Consumer hardware' is not in the abstract, which says only 'single GPU'. The accuracy cost and the sensitivity to routing mispredictions are not reported there. R6 shows that quantization, another route to cheaper deployment, degrades for MoE.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: 'Up to' maxima against selected baselines are not typical performance. The step to 'consumer hardware more feasible' is an extrapolation by the finding, not a result of the abstract.
finding.supporting_excerpt: reducing GPU memory usage by up to 93.72% and improving inference throughput by up to 10x over strong offloading baselines on a single GPU.

finding.claim: The Science findings present MoE mainly as an efficiency success and do not cover training instability. Reinforcement-learning post-training of MoE models is reported to suffer routing-induced instability and even collapse. Mechanistic explanations were described as lacking until recently. This is relevant to S1, S4 and S2, which imply routing and specialization are largely handled by recent designs.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstracts report instability and collapse in MoE RL and a training-inference routing mismatch. The proposed remedy, R3, comes from a single paper. Omitting this risk gives an unbalanced picture of MoE maturity.
finding.supporting_excerpt: in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, the routing mechanism often introduces instability, even leading to catastrophic RL training collapse.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

limitations: Only 12 papers, abstracts only (no full text); several abstracts are truncated (e.g., GrMoE, AdapterMoE).
Half are arXiv preprints that are not peer reviewed.

No papers directly on hardware cost, memory footprint, inference serving, communication/bandwidth bottlenecks, or comparison with dense or other alternatives at frontier scale, so these are evidence gaps rather than findings.
Several results are small-scale or off-domain (image classification, crop disease, recommendation), limiting relevance to commercial LLM MoE.
No company-level evidence was provided, so no company-specific risks are asserted.
Search was risk-oriented but narrow; the stated papers' own proposed fixes may overstate how much of each problem remains.
Only titles and abstracts were reviewed. Results inside papers, such as ablations, baselines and benchmark details, were not checked.
Many of the cited papers are 2025-2026 arXiv preprints without peer review, and citation counts are missing for most. I could not assess their reliability beyond the abstracts.
Challenges rest on the supplied 24-paper evidence list. Contradicting literature outside it, for example on Soft MoE's behaviour in autoregressive language modelling, could not be cited.
I did not challenge S6, S8 or S9. S6 and S8 are consistent with their abstracts, though S6 is labelled conservatively. S9 is vaguely worded ('satisfactory performance') but matches its abstract.

limitations: Only 12 posts in a 7-day window matched the topic keywords; several (all @ETNOWlive posts) were about Goldman Sachs' India market commentary and matched only on 'Moe', contributing nothing about mixture of experts.

No posts from major semiconductor, memory, or standards accounts (@nvidia, @AMD, @MicronTech, @JEDEC, etc.) mentioned MoE, so there is no signal here about hardware/infrastructure implications of sparse expert models.
Most MoE posts come from one aggregator account (@Decoded08) and one agent (@thePandaily), reducing source independence.
Benchmark numbers and performance claims are as-posted promotional/company figures; linked articles and papers were not read.
Engagement was low across relevant posts (0-13), indicating limited attention rather than confirmation.

sources.title: Real-Time Multimodal Classroom Observation System with Transcript-Enhanced Cross-Attention Fusion and Rule-Based Adaptive Sampling (Edge-Only Execution) [US20260369059A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    An edge-only classroom observation system performs real-time multimodal classroom event detection while limiting transmission of raw classroom media. An edge device captures classroom video and audio, generates transcript data locally using an on-device speech-to-text engine, and produces video, audio, and transcript token embeddings. A transformer encoder fuses the embeddings through cross-modal attention in a unified attention architecture that does not use learned gating networks or mixture-of-experts routing to select modality-specific experts. A deterministic adaptive sampling engine adjusts camera or microphone capture parameters using threshold rules based on locally measured brightness and audio level or noise conditions, without reinforcement learning capture control. A quantized inference pipeline classifies classroom behavioral or instructional events locally and publishes abstract event metadata to a dashboard while withholding raw video, audio, and transcript text from transmission for event classification.

sources.title: Reinforcement learning based expert routing for mixture of experts language models [US12792925B1]
sources.abstract: Embodiments disclosed herein may use reinforcement learning techniques to train a gating network and optimize routing policy. Reinforcement learning may allow for an immediate reward (or penalty as the case may be) such that the desired actions can be rewarded and undesired actions can be penalized. The routing policy optimized using reinforcement learning may move away from the inflexible approach of the conventional gating networks and offer a desired level of flexibility for any type of query. Additionally, the gating network may be continuously trained upon deployment.

sources.title: DYNAMIC PARALLELISM FOR LANGUAGE MODEL INFERENCE [US20260350380A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Various examples relate to dynamic parallelism for language model inference. A pool of processing units is reconfigured between different parallelism modes during inference. In a first mode for attention computation, contextual memory data is distributed across processing units. After attention computation, the units are reprovisioned into a second mode with multi-dimensional parallelism, having tensor parallelism and sparse computation dimensions. The second mode enables processing tokens through neural networks in a sparse computation architecture. For dense models without mixture-of-experts, the sparse computation dimension equals one, allowing graceful degradation to tensor-parallel execution. Collective communication operations may facilitate transitions between modes while maintaining mathematical equivalence with non-distributed computation.

sources.title: STAGED MIXED PARALLELISM REASONING METHOD AND SYSTEM FOR MOE SPARSE LARGE MODELS [US20260340345A1]
sources.abstract: The present disclosure provides a staged mixed parallelism reasoning method and system for an MoE sparse large model. The method includes: controlling the MoE sparse large model to execute the following steps layer by layer in a prefill stage: adding first MoE layer model parameters running based on a tensor parallelism strategy to each device while acquiring an expert number of each token of a prompt data sequence; then performing expert parallelism computation based on second MoE layer model parameters in each device running based on an expert parallelism strategy; restoring the tokens to device initial positions and releasing the second MoE layer model parameters; and sending a predicted token output by a last layer of the model to a first layer to execute reasoning in a decoding stage according to the predicted token and the first MoE layer model parameters in each device. The present disclosure can solve the problems that a parallelism strategy adopted by an existing MoE sparse large model reasoning technology has poor adaptability to the prefill stage and the decoding stage and large communication overhead.

sources.abstract: Embodiments of the present invention disclose a mixture-of-experts model optimization method, apparatus, and device. In the embodiments of the present invention, the method comprises: acquiring an average number of tokens of a mixture-of-experts model, the tokens being basic units used by the mixture-of-experts model to process input data; determining N times the average number of tokens of the mixture-of-experts model, N being an integer or a decimal greater than 1; and requesting allocation of target GPU memory on the basis of N times the average number of of tokens, the target GPU memory being configured to store tokens during a forward-propagation process. In the method, when allocation of GPU memory is requested during forward propagation, the GPU memory is allocated on the basis of N times the average number of tokens, thereby solving the problem of GPU memory fragmentation, reducing the GPU memory occupied by the mixture-of-experts model, and achieving optimization of the mixture-of-experts model.

sources.title: Method and System for Agent-Based Semantic Characterization and Self-Supervised Validation of Electronic Components Using Simulation and Expert Feedback [US20260330113A1]
sources.abstract: A system and method for semantic characterization and validation of electronic components using a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) agent architecture. The system comprises: (1) a content orchestration agent responsible for extraction and normalization of device datasheet information, and (2) a simulation-generation agent which produces subcircuit models using a structured grammar and validates them via self-supervised SPICE simulations. The agents collaborate iteratively to construct scenarios reflective of real-world operating conditions, bridging the gap between idealized datasheet curves and actual component behavior. Simulation results are analyzed using clustering algorithms to form a performance taxonomy, enabling deterministic classification, similarity analysis, and circuit design recommendations.

NPU-Friendly Token Routing for Mixture-of-Experts Based Large Language Models on Edge Devices [US20260320352A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A neural processing unit (NPU) controls the routing of input tokens to experts in a mixture-of-experts (MoE) network. The NPU generates a routing table having a batch dimension of Bs and an expert dimension of N. Each element in the routing table is a probability value of routing an input token to an expert. The NPU further generates an expert selection vector indicating K top-ranked experts for each input token by performing quantization operations and rectified linear operations on N probability values along the expert dimension of the routing table with respect to the input token. The NPU further generates N sets of one-hot expert projection vectors for respective experts based on the routing table and expert selection vectors for the Bs input tokens. The N sets of one-hot expert project vectors are used to select the input tokens to dispatch to the experts.

sources.abstract: The invention provides a MoE-BERT auxiliary dimension reduction hierarchical distributed multi-target chaotic game network construction type power system scheduling method, a medium and a processor. According to the method, firstly, a multi-target scheduling model considering power generation energy consumption, carbon emission, renewable energy operation and maintenance energy consumption and energy storage charging and discharging penalty energy consumption is constructed; secondly, dividing the centralized system into a plurality of layered distributed sub-regions step by step by adopting a two-time bus tearing method, and solving a non-dominated solution in each region by utilizing a multi-target chaos game; then, based on historical solution data, MoE-BERT is trained, a mapping relation between an objective function value and a non-dominated solution is learned, and after a chaotic game is iterated to a threshold value, a candidate solution is generated to replace a partially redundant iteration process. And finally, taking the candidate solution as an initial solution of a subsequent chaotic game method, and continuing to search and update the non-dominated solution set. According to the method, the layered and distributed multi-target scheduling problem in the network construction type power system can be solved, dimensionality reduction and rapid solution of the scheduling problem are realized, and the solution efficiency is improved.

The method is helpful for improving the calibration coverage quality during quantification after training of routing experts.

sources.abstract: The invention belongs to the field of wireless communication and sensing integration, and particularly relates to a multi-mode sensing integration method for a high mobility network. According to the joint optimization method based on the RL-H-MoE architecture, strict physical and gradient decoupling of time scheduling and space mapping is achieved, and gradient conflicts commonly existing in multi-task learning are effectively avoided. By introducing the semantic AoI to realize the optimal sensing strategy triggered by the event, the scheme can realize the long-term energy cost minimization of the system on the premise of strictly ensuring the physical layer communication link connection and ultra-low sensing error (the tracking precision is comparable with a pure vision continuous opening scheme) (the energy is saved by more than 40% compared with a pure vision scheme); and the method has extremely high 6G V2I actual deployment potential.

sources.title: Adaptive semantic learning pathological image classification method based on sparse expert routing [CN122841827A]
sources.abstract: The invention discloses an adaptive semantic learning pathological image classification method based on sparse expert routing, and belongs to the technical field of pathological images. As a pathological image has significant morphological heterogeneity, an existing multi-instance learning method aggregates different tissue modes to a shared feature space, and difference contributions of various tissue structures are difficult to effectively characterize. According to the invention, a learnable prototype construction module LPC and a sparse expert routing module SER are designed. Wherein the LPC module constructs a learnable semantic prototype; the SER module realizes sparse distribution from examples to an expert network, so that different experts focus on a specific organization mode, and pathological image classification is completed. In order to promote experts to learn heterogeneous features, an information bottleneck optimization module IBO is introduced, and ASSE is optimized in combination with classification loss. Experimental results show that the morphological heterogeneity problem in the pathological image can be effectively relieved, and the classification performance and the model generalization ability are improved.

Inputting into a multi-scale time Patch encoder to obtain time representation; inputting the topology, electrical and event/weather similarity information of the current scheduling period into a graph encoder to construct a time-varying adjacent matrix and aggregate time representation, and outputting graph relationship representation; fusing the two representations to obtain an object-level operation representation; inputting the object-level operation representation, the event semantics, the structured event and the working condition statistical vector into a fusion encoder, and outputting an object fusion representation after event enhancement; inputting the working condition statistical vector and the object fusion representation after event enhancement into a working condition sensing sparse expert route header, and outputting an object prediction representation; and outputting a multi-task prediction and interpretable result based on the prediction representation, and generating a next scheduling cycle scheduling instruction. According to the invention, accurate prediction and interpretable scheduling control of the source network load storage system are realized.

sources.title: Protein stability prediction method and device based on sparse mixed expert and storage medium [CN122842715A]
sources.abstract: The invention discloses a protein stability prediction method and device based on sparse mixed experts and a storage medium. The prediction method comprises the following steps: firstly, extracting protein sequence embedding characteristics by using a plurality of tested medium parameter protein language models (PLM); constructing a core feature vector through feature compression and wild type-mutant element-by-element difference calculation; dynamic adaptive fusion of multi-source features is realized based on a sparse hybrid expert (MoE) architecture; accurate prediction of protein stability free energy change and melting temperature change is completed through the regression model. According to the method, the technical problems of one-sided feature capture of a single protein language model, high calculation cost of a large-parameter model, model over-fitting in a small sample scene and the like are solved, and through collaborative fusion of medium-parameter PLM, the calculation resource threshold is greatly reduced while the accuracy and the stability of a prediction result are ensured to be improved.

sources.abstract: The invention provides an expert parallel load balancing method, device and equipment, a medium and a product, and relates to the technical field of artificial intelligence, in particular to the technical fields of cloud computing, large models, computing power and the like. The expert parallel load balancing method comprises the following steps: grouping a plurality of GPUs deployed with MoE models so as to determine hot-spot GPUs and cold-spot GPUs; on the basis of the topological relation among the plurality of GPUs and the original load capacity of each GPU, determining an expert to be copied in host experts deployed on the hotspot GPU, and determining a target GPU in the cold-spot GPU; copying the expert to be copied to obtain a visitor expert, and loading the visitor expert to the target GPU; and shunting the original traffic of the to-be-copied expert by adopting the visitor expert. According to the invention, resource overhead during load balancing can be reduced.

sources.title: MoE model heterogeneous low-power-consumption scheduling method and system based on expert activation risk assessment [CN122819489A]
sources.abstract: The invention discloses a MoE model heterogeneous low-power-consumption scheduling method and system based on expert activation risk assessment. The problem of high power consumption during large model reasoning in the prior art is mainly solved. The method comprises the following steps: acquiring expert activation information according to a scheduling period; the future activation probability and prediction uncertainty are calculated, and the low-power-consumption state risk is calculated in combination with the wake-up cost, the misprediction penalty and the PIM bottom execution cost; dividing the experts into four different scheduling states according to the risk, and generating a distribution or low-power-consumption control instruction; according to the actual activation state, the actual lexical element number and the deviation between the actual execution state and the prediction result, recording a feedback event, correcting prediction parameters, risk assessment or a state switching threshold value, and based on the results, repeating a scheduling cycle until the reasoning task is completed. PIM is preferentially adopted for execution for experts which are low in activation probability, high in prediction uncertainty and activated by a small number of lexical elements in the future. According to the method, invalid energy consumption and frequent wakeup can be reduced under the delay controllable condition, and the method can be used for an NPU-PIM heterogeneous reasoning platform.

sources.title: Hybrid expert model pruning method and device and terminal equipment [CN122819345A]
sources.abstract: The invention relates to a hybrid expert model pruning method and device and terminal equipment, and the method comprises the steps: controlling a target hybrid expert MoE model to carry out the forward reasoning, and enabling the target MoE model to comprise a plurality of MoE layers; obtaining an average routing entropy of all lexical elements in each MoE layer; under the constraint of a target pruning number of the target MoE model, based on the average routing entropy of each MoE layer, distributing a layer pruning number for each MoE layer, the layer pruning number being in positive correlation with the average routing entropy; and on the basis of the layer pruning number of each MoE layer, performing expert pruning on the target MoE model to obtain a pruned MoE model. Through the method and the device, the problem that the performance of the MoE model is reduced or the MoE model cannot be fully compressed due to uniform expert pruning is solved, and the technical effect of reducing performance loss of the MoE model caused by expert pruning is achieved.

sources.title: Anonymous user-oriented session recommendation method, computer storage medium, program and electronic equipment [CN122817446A]
sources.abstract: The invention discloses an anonymous user-oriented session recommendation method, a computer storage medium, a program and electronic equipment. The recommendation method is a de-noising architecture based on an expert hybrid model MoE. Firstly, orthogonal decoupling of project ID representation and modal features is achieved in a multi-modal representation space, multi-expert denoising network collaboration is further designed based on an expert hybrid model MoE, context features are captured on different scales, and potential preference distribution is restored in a multi-scale and multi-granularity collaboration mode. According to the method, the diversity of fine grit is reserved, deep semantic abstraction is realized, so that relevant and rich diversified recommendation results are generated, and the diversity of sequence data is improved.

draft.summary: Research on mixture of experts is growing very quickly. Papers with the exact topic phrase rose from 723 in 2024 to 2,299 in 2025 (+218%), and 2026 year-to-date is still running about 216% above the same point in 2025. Patent publications are also rising (352 by 26 Oct 2026 vs 166 a year earlier), mostly on routing, parallelism, pruning and quantization for deployment. The Science findings support efficiency gains in training, but the Risk challenges narrow several of them: key results come from single preprints, self-reported comparisons or small-scale tests. Commercial evidence is thin: two SEC filers describe MoE products and X posts show open-weight model releases, but these are company claims, not proof of customer adoption or returns. The main uncertainty is whether the training-compute advantage carries through to deployment cost and stable post-training at scale.
draft.plain_summary: Mixture of experts is a way of building AI models so that only a small part of the model works on each task, which can save computing effort. Research and patent filings are growing very fast and several organisations have released models built this way, so it looks like it is really taking off. The main thing that could hold it back is that these models can be hard to train stably and expensive to run in memory, and many of the reported savings come from single studies.

themes.name: MoE as an efficiency architecture for large AI models

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Research and patent counts are rising steeply (S1, S8, P1), and X posts show several open-weight MoE releases in one week (X2, X1, X5). These X posts are unverified social signals. Deployment bottlenecks (memory, quantization, RL post-training instability) are documented (S3, R1, R6, C8), so near-term progress is more likely to be about making MoE cheaper to serve than about new capability. Evidence is partly from single preprints.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: If deployment methods such as expert pruning, predictive caching and hardware-aware scheduling mature (S9, S12, P4, P5), MoE could stay a default way to scale model capacity. The cited results are best-case, single-paper figures (C7), and the unresolved failure modes of expert collapse and routing instability (R3, R2) may limit this. Nothing here shows the architecture will stay dominant.

horizons.label: assumption
horizons.assessment: The evidence says little directly about 3-5 years. Continued patent growth and the spread to other domains (P3, X4) suggest sustained interest, but the other-domain uses differ in what they call MoE (C6), and many fixes are validated only at small scale (R8). Any long-term view is an assumption.

bull.label: forecast
bull.narrative: Fine-grained and open MoE designs keep delivering better quality per unit of compute (S8, S11). Deployment tooling closes the memory and inference gap (S9, S12, P4, P5). Open-weight releases and growing filings (X2, P1) make MoE a standard building block, and commercial users (M1, M2) expand.

base.label: forecast
base.narrative: MoE remains widely researched and patented, with steady releases of open models (X2, X5). Gains are real in training compute (S1), but they are offset by memory, communication and quantization costs (C1, R6) and by routing and stability issues that need workarounds (R3, R7). Commercial use grows unevenly, led by a few early filers (M3, M4).

bear.label: forecast
bear.narrative: Routing instability, expert collapse and RL post-training collapse stay unsolved (R1, R2, R3, C8). Deployment savings prove smaller than headline numbers (C2, C7, R6), and many improvements fail to transfer from small-scale tests to production scale (R8). Research volume grows without a matching commercial payoff (M4, T1).
